title: About
text:
This website was developed as a project towards the requirements of the Graduate Academic Certificate in Science Communication at McMaster University (2026–2027).
The website’s structure was initially developed with the assistance of Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5, which I used to generate a template for the Quarto documents. I subsequently adapted and customized this template to suit the specific objectives and content of the project.
The interactive visualizations were inspired by two projects in particular. The data manipulation visualizations draw inspiration from Andrew Heiss’s (2024) blog post, Visualizing {dplyr}’s mutate(), summarize(), group_by(), and ungroup() with animations. The interactive design and emphasis on learning through experimentation were influenced by Vi Hart and Nicky Case’s (2014) Parable of the Polygons.
The example dataset used throughout the website comes from the lterdatasampler R package, developed by contributors to the Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) Network. This package provides educational datasets collected through LTER research sites.
Additional resources that informed the development of the website, including resources on R programming, data visualization, and Quarto website development, are listed below.






Hart, V., & Case, N. (2014). Parable of the polygons. https://ncase.me/polygons/
Heiss, A. (2024, April 4). Visualizing {dplyr}’s mutate(), summarize(), group_by(), and ungroup() with animations. https://doi.org/10.59350/d2sz4-w4e25





Horst, A., Brun, J., Guo, S., Logan, A., Ran, L., Sternberg, S., & Zhao, K. (2023). lterdatasampler: Educational dataset examples from the Long Term Ecological Research Program (Version 0.1.1) [R package]. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.lterdatasampler
Kosourova, E. (2023, March 6). How to write functions in R (with 18 code examples). Dataquest. https://www.dataquest.io/blog/write-functions-in-r/
ggplot smooth line: Add a trend line with geom_smooth. (2026, June 27). Datanovia. https://www.datanovia.com/learn/data-visualization/ggplot2/smooth-line





Çetinkaya-Rundel, M., & Wickham, C. (n.d.). 14 Websites. In Quarto: The practical guide. https://quarto-tdg.org/websites

title: Full Workflow
text:
Start by loading packages.

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(lterdatasampler)
library(knitr)

Then load in the data.

data(pie_crab)

Create a table of summary statistics.

# create summary table
summ_tble <- pie_crab %>% 
  select(site, size, latitude) %>% 
  group_by(site) %>% 
  summarise(mean_size = mean(size), 
            latitude = unique(latitude),
            sd_size = sd(size)) 

# make the table print with a caption
summ_tble %>% 
  kable()

Then plot it.

ggplot(data = pie_crab, 
       aes(x = latitude, y = size)) + 
  geom_jitter(color = "grey50", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_point(data = summ_tble, 
             aes(x = latitude, y = mean_size), 
             color = "grey30", size = 3) + 
  geom_smooth(formula = y~x, method = "lm",
              color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Latitude", y = "Carapace size (mm)") +
  theme_classic()







Figure 1: Fiddler crab carapace size (mm) in relation to latitude. Light grey points represent individual observations, while black larger points show mean values for sample sites. Smooth shows positive relationship between carapace size and latitude.
